summary: A CBOR Web Token claims set is normally protected by a signature, MAC, or encryption. This RFC defines the Unprotected CWT Claims Set (UCCS), a format and CBOR tag for carrying claims without that protection, for use where security is provided by other means such as a secure channel.

plainLanguage.summary: A note can be carried in a locked box, or handed over in a safe room. UCCS is the note with no lock of its own, used when the room is already safe.

questions: when can i use an unprotected cwt claims set
subtitle: A CBOR tag for sending CWT claims without a signature, when a secure channel already protects them.

tldr.problem: A CBOR Web Token is always wrapped in a COSE envelope, which adds signature or MAC overhead even when the two parties already share a secure channel that gives the same protection.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the Unprotected CWT Claims Set (UCCS): a plain claims map marked with CBOR tag 601, to be conveyed only inside a Secure Channel, plus media types and a CDDL definition.
tldr.outcome: Claims can be conveyed economically in Remote Attestation Procedures (RATS) when the channel supplies authentication, integrity and confidentiality, but they lose that protection once they leave the channel.

today: RFC 9781 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2025 and, per the metadata, it has not been obsoleted or updated. It defines UCCS and its tag 601, and limits use to scopes where the security of the Secure Channel has been analysed.

sections.title: Claims Without a COSE Wrapper
sections.content:
A CBOR Web Token (CWT), specified in RFC 8392, is always wrapped in a COSE envelope, which provides data origin authentication, integrity protection and optional encryption. If two parties already have a mutually secured channel with the required properties, they can reuse it, and the COSE protection can be omitted.

This RFC allocates a CBOR tag to mark Unprotected CWT Claims Sets (UCCS) and discusses when it may be used, in the scope of Remote Attestation Procedures (RATS, RFC 9334). It does not change RFC 8392: a CWT does not use this tag, and the UCCS tag is an alternative to COSE protection plus a CWT tag. The contents of a UCCS can also be used to build a CWT that some entity signs to vouch for them.
sections.plainLanguage: If you and a friend already talk through a private tunnel, you do not need to also seal every note in an envelope. UCCS is the note without the envelope.

sections.title: What a Secure Channel Must Provide
sections.content:
A Secure Channel must supply the security properties COSE would otherwise supply. The RFC compares UCCS to JWTs that use the algorithm none, citing RFC 8725 that this can be acceptable when a transport layer such as TLS protects the JWT end to end. The channel's cryptographic strength should be at least as strong as any keys it protects in transport.

For the purposes of the RFC, the channel gives mutual authentication, integrity protection and confidentiality. Replay protection can be added with a nonce claim such as Nonce (claim 10). Examples are PCIe IDE (Integrity and Data Encryption) and a TLS tunnel. Channels are often set up by a handshake that derives a session key, such as the TLS handshake of RFC 8446.

The mechanisms that establish the channel are out of scope. For environments other than RATS, similar considerations need to be documented before UCCS is used.
sections.plainLanguage: The private tunnel has to do three jobs: check who is on each end, stop anyone changing the note, and keep it secret.

sections.title: Rules for RATS Conveyance
sections.content:
Any RATS role can send or receive a UCCS. The receiver MUST authenticate the sender when the channel is established, and the channel MUST provide integrity. For confidentiality the receiving side MUST be authenticated too, which happens when both sides authenticate mutually. Using UCCS tag 601 outside the RATS context MUST come with additional instructions and security considerations.

Ultimately the receiver's policy decides whether to accept a UCCS and what kind of channel it must negotiate; the policy itself is out of scope. Where an Attesting Environment is an endpoint of the channel, a Relying Party generally expects it to be hardened, for example a TEE or a TPM.

When a UCCS leaves the channel it is only as protected as any other unprotected data in the Verifier environment, and a forwarded UCCS is treated as if it originated at the receiver. A fully formed CWT inside the channel keeps its COSE envelope, so the channel does not endorse it the way it does a UCCS.
sections.plainLanguage: The person receiving the note must know exactly who sent it. Once the note leaves the safe room, it is just an ordinary piece of paper again.

sections.title: Delegated Attestation and Privacy
sections.content:
In delegated attestation, a sub-Attester that has no signing keys sends a UCCS over a Secure Channel, such as local inter-process communication, to a lead Attester. The lead Attester hashes the UCCS and protects that hash with its signing key for Evidence, for example using a Detached-Submodule-Digest or Detached EAT Bundle.

For privacy, a privacy-preserving channel can give protection equivalent to COSE, but only within the life of the session. An Attester must consider whether the UCCS it returns compromises privacy. For instance, an EAT UEID claim lets a Verifier correlate UCCS from one Attesting Environment across many sessions, which can be fine for a factory sensor and unacceptable for a child's device.
sections.plainLanguage: A helper with no stamp passes its note to the boss in a safe room, and the boss stamps a summary of it. Also, a note with your name on it lets people recognise you every time.

sections.title: The UCCS Format and CDDL
sections.content:
A UCCS is a CBOR map of Claims (Claim Key and Claim Value pairs) as defined by the CWT Claims Registry. Tagged, it is 601(...). The normative CDDL in Appendix A defines UCCS-Untagged = Claims-Set and UCCS-Tagged = #6.601(UCCS-Untagged), because RFC 8392 gave no CDDL for CWT Claims Sets.

The same CDDL can describe JWT claims sets (RFC 7519) by switching a feature from cbor to json. An unsigned JSON claims set is called a Unprotected JWT Claims Set (UJCS). Appendix C adds UCCS and UJCS tokens to Entity Attestation Tokens (RFC 9711).

The informative example turns the claims set from RFC 8392 into a UCCS simply by enclosing it with tag 601.
sections.plainLanguage: It is the same list of facts as before, with a sticker numbered 601 on top that says 'this one travels without a lock'.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA allocated CBOR tag 601 in the CBOR Tags registry, with a map (Claims-Set) as the data item and the semantics Unprotected CWT Claims Set.

It also registered the media type application/uccs+cbor (file extension .uccs) and the media type application/ujcs+json (file extension .ujcs), and a CoAP Content-Format for application/uccs+cbor with ID 601.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of names now has entries for the new sticker number and for the two kinds of file.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of CBOR and of RFC 8392 apply, with the Secure Channel taking the place of COSE. The RFC is explicit that UCCS is not intended for use in a scope where a scope-specific security discussion has not been conducted, vetted and approved. To use the tag elsewhere, the channel or application protocol MUST specify the roles of the endpoints so the security properties are well defined.

General points include protecting the key material used to set up the channel, not using one key for more than one algorithm, respecting key usage limits, and not using Evidence in a UCCS to support trust in the credentials that set up the same channel, which would be circular. The Verifier needs to be sure that key management for the channel is acceptable. A table points to algorithm-specific considerations in RFC 9053 for AES-CBC-MAC, AES-GCM, AES-CCM and ChaCha20/Poly1305.
sections.plainLanguage: The safe room only counts if its locks are good, and a note cannot be used to prove the room is safe.

data.title: CWT claims set enclosed with tag 601
data.code:
601(
  {
    / iss / 1: "coap://as.example.com",
    / sub / 2: "erikw",
    / aud / 3: "coap://light.example.com",
    / exp / 4: 1444064944,
    / nbf / 5: 1443944944,
    / iat / 6: 1443944944,
    / cti / 7: h'0b71'
  }
)
